summary:
Saint Lucia's High Court decriminalised same-sex conduct in July 2025, striking down the criminal provision as unconstitutional in Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia. Human Rights Watch reported the judgment on 31 July 2025 and the Associated Press carried it as well. The case was part of strategic constitutional litigation brought across the Eastern Caribbean rather than a legislative amendment, and the provision struck down was the colonial-era statute that had governed same-sex conduct.

For a visitor, the practical effect is direct: consensual same-sex conduct between adults no longer carries criminal exposure in Saint Lucia. Before the judgment, the statutory prohibition applied to anyone present on the island, residents and visitors alike, and that specific criminal risk ended with the court's declaration of unconstitutionality.

The judgment addressed criminal liability only. Matters such as legal gender recognition, relationship or marriage recognition, hate-crime protection and anti-discrimination coverage are not addressed by the sources available for this record, and a visitor should not read the decriminalisation ruling as settling them.

Official engagement with LGBTI rights is documented at the enforcement level. United and Strong St Lucia reported that a human-rights sensitisation session for law enforcement was held in Castries on 19 May 2015, bringing together officers of the Royal St Lucia Police Force, Air and Sea Ports, Customs and staff of the Bordelais Correctional Facility, alongside CariFLAGS, the Canadian HIV-AIDS Legal Network and Maurice Tomlinson. The session built on sensitisation work carried out in 2014.
tangentialFactors:
The decriminalisation ruling did not arise in isolation. It followed a pattern of constitutional challenges filed across the Eastern Caribbean, in which colonial-era prohibitions on same-sex conduct were challenged as unconstitutional; the Saint Lucia judgment is one product of that regional litigation strategy.

Caribbean LGBTI organisations have asserted control over how their issues are framed externally. In April 2017, United and Strong of St Lucia and ECADE (the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality) publicly protested a PinkNews item of 28 March 2017 that presented regional sexuality under the banner 'Nothing about us without us', documenting sustained civil-society pushback against outsider framing of Caribbean LGBT issues.
localsOnly:
Human-rights sensitisation training for law enforcement has been delivered domestically. The session held in Castries on 19 May 2015 convened officers from the Royal St Lucia Police Force, Air and Sea Ports, Customs and the Bordelais Correctional Facility with CariFLAGS, the Canadian HIV-AIDS Legal Network and Maurice Tomlinson, and extended sensitisation work begun in 2014.

The constitutional challenge that produced decriminalisation was brought by Saint Lucian litigants against the Attorney General of Saint Lucia, Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia, and the relief was granted by the Saint Lucia High Court rather than by an act of the legislature.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust case digest covering Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403). The ruling itself is corroborated by Human Rights Watch and the Associated Press, but the digest's fuller treatment of the court's reasoning remains unresolved for this record.

Rules on legal gender recognition and gender markers on documents are not sourced in the available material for Saint Lucia and are unresolved here. The same applies to recognition of same-sex partnerships or marriage, to hate-crime provisions covering gender identity or expression, and to statutory anti-discrimination protection. No source in this inventory speaks to entry, visa or customs screening practices that could expose a visitor's gender identity or expression.
